title: US Puts 17 Million More SPR Barrels on the Block as Ukraine Hits Russia's Diesel Supply
subhead: The US opened a fresh solicitation for 17 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve as crude holds above $100, while Ukraine's drone strike on Rosneft's Ryazan refinery drew a public rebuke from Trump and deepened the global diesel squeeze. Brent trades near $110.

sections.heading: Washington Tries Again on the SPR — and Refiners May Not Bite
sections.body:
The US Department of Energy issued a request for proposals on Friday for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, part of the 172 million barrels Washington committed under the IEA's 400-million-barrel emergency action announced in March, OilPrice reports. The SPR currently holds about 283 million barrels; if companies take the full volume before repayments arrive, inventories would fall to roughly 266 million barrels — squarely inside the 250-300 million range generally treated as the reserve's operational minimum.

The catch is demand for the oil itself. When DOE offered the final tranche of its March commitment in June, it required companies to return borrowed crude with premiums of as much as 24%, and firms agreed to take only about 500,000 barrels. Friday's solicitation follows the IEA's Thursday decision to accelerate roughly 100 million barrels still outstanding from March, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel. US commercial crude inventories have fallen more than 51 million barrels over the past 26 weeks, per API estimates.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is draining its emergency buffer into a market it cannot fully supply. The June flop shows the exchange mechanism is unattractive to refiners at current repayment terms — the same terms now being recycled suggest the release may not translate into the barrels the market needs.

sections.heading: Ukraine Reopens Strikes on Russian Refineries — and Washington Objects
sections.body:
Ukrainian drones struck Rosneft's Ryazan refinery, a facility accounting for about 5% of Russia's national refinery throughput, after President Zelensky told the Financial Times, 'The block is out. We're done,' signaling the collapse of a short-lived pause in refinery attacks. President Trump responded on Newsmax that the strikes are 'a disgrace' that 'only lead to higher prices,' adding he was 'not a fan' of Zelensky and that 'they've destroyed that country' — an unusually direct rupture with Kyiv.

The strikes land squarely in a diesel market already under severe strain. Trump had announced a Kyiv-Moscow ceasefire on Sunday that neither side confirmed; Russian forces continued striking targets in Ukraine, and the Ryazan attack resumed the refinery campaign days later. Diesel and refined-product tightness is now the binding constraint in the global fuel market, and both wars would need to end for the pressure to ease, as OilPrice's Irina Slav notes.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is targeting the one commodity the West most needs — diesel — while its largest backer publicly sides against the tactic. That contradiction limits how far Kyiv can push refinery strikes without straining Western political support.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia's Houthi Problem Keeps Washington on the Sidelines
sections.body:
The Houthis hit Aramco's Dhahran headquarters on Tuesday night — the building housing the operations center for Aramco's rigs, pipelines, refineries, and export terminals — setting fire across several floors, and have kept Riyadh's main airport shut into the weekend with nearly half of all Saudi flights cancelled, per OilPrice. The same week, a missile struck King Khalid's terminals in Riyadh and killed 13 people, including an American.

Washington's rule since September is to stay out of the Saudi-Houthi war as long as the Houthis hit only Saudi targets — a posture that preserves US firepower but leaves Riyadh exposed. Meanwhile, Brent trades at about $109.9 and WTI at roughly $101.4, with the Opec basket near $111.6 and India's basket above $121, per OilPrice's live pricing.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthis can degrade Saudi export infrastructure without triggering direct US retaliation, meaning Gulf oil flows carry a persistent, cheaply-imposed risk premium that no ceasefire on the table removes.

sections.heading: Europe and Asia Burn Coal Again as Gas Stays Unaffordable
sections.body:
The global LNG crunch has made Europe's remaining coal plants profitable again. In Germany, a key lignite profitability measure jumped to as much as $72 (64 euros) per MWh this month, from zero a year ago, per Energy Aspects estimates cited by Bloomberg. The IEA's Coal Mid-Year Update 2026 now expects European coal demand at 276 million tons in 2026, down from 292 million last year but higher than previously forecast, precisely because high gas prices have slowed the decline in Germany and Poland.

In Asia, South Korea — the world's third-largest LNG importer — will lean more on coal and nuclear this winter. Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Kim Sungwhan told Bloomberg, 'In the short term, we are in a situation where we must somehow reduce LNG demand.' South Korean coal-fired supply already jumped 40% in April, the biggest rise since August 2019, per Reuters-cited data. Chinese underground gas storage was 80% full at end-September, according to Rystad Energy's Xiong Wei, giving Beijing a buffer ahead of winter. European storage sits at just 74%, versus above 86% for the previous five-year average.
sections.whyItMatters: The energy transition is being quietly deferred across both Europe and Northeast Asia as economics override climate targets. Coal is back as the winter insurance policy, and a colder-than-expected season would force harder choices.

sections.heading: PetroChina's Trading Arm Set for a Record $3 Billion
sections.body:
PetroChina International, the trading vehicle of Asia's biggest oil and gas producer, is set to book more than $3 billion (20 billion yuan) in gross trading profit for 2026, anonymous trade sources told Reuters. The Hormuz crisis and subsequent price spikes drove exceptional margins across PetroChina's crude, fuels, and LNG trading divisions, with crude and LNG benefiting from high volatility and arbitrage opportunities. PetroChina reported record first-half profit attributable to shareholders, up 22% year over year to $15.5 billion.

The windfall is not China-specific. TotalEnergies expects strong third-quarter results, Shell said its indicative Q3 refining margin nearly doubled sequentially to a record $42 per barrel from $24, and Norway's Equinor expects 'unusually strong European refining margins' to push its marketing division above $400 million in guidance.
sections.whyItMatters: Supply crises redistribute profit toward those who can move molecules, not those who produce them. State and private majors alike are converting volatility into record trading income — a quiet confirmation that the current market rewards logistics over ownership.

sections.heading: India Tilts Its Duty Structure Toward Diesel Exports
sections.body:
India nearly halved its diesel export duty for the next two weeks — from 16 rupees ($0.17) to 8.5 rupees ($0.09) per liter — while hiking the gasoline export levy fivefold to 2.5 rupees ($0.026) per liter, effective October 16, per the Times of India. The jet fuel export duty was left unchanged at 10.5 rupees per liter.

The move is designed to push more diesel onto a world market reeling from a diesel crunch, while discouraging gasoline exports. India introduced these duties in March at the height of the Middle East crisis and has reviewed them every fortnight since. Oil Minister Hardeep Puri said in September that India would keep exporting diesel to ease the global fuel crunch, noting the country's refining capacity continues to expand.
sections.whyItMatters: India is using tax policy as a supply tool, effectively subsidizing diesel flows to a strained global market while safeguarding domestic gasoline. It shows how mid-tier refining powers can shape product balances without touching volumes directly.

sections.heading: Washington Courts Central Asia for Energy and Minerals
sections.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to Samarkand, Uzbekistan on October 19 to meet the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, accompanied by a delegation of more than 100 US companies pursuing energy, critical minerals, and infrastructure deals, per OilPrice. The C5+1 format, launched in 2015, runs a Critical Minerals Dialogue in parallel; the size of the business delegation signals Washington wants financed projects rather than another declaration.

Central Asia holds significant critical mineral deposits, and the push offers the five republics alternatives to Russian and Chinese influence — though the region is balancing among all three powers. The agenda also escalates US rivalry with neighboring Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: With Gulf energy routes disrupted, Washington is widening the map of where it secures supply and processing capacity. Whether the Central Asian republics hedge or commit will shape who controls the next decade of critical mineral flows.

bottomLine: Two pressures defined the day. On supply, the US put another 17 million SPR barrels on offer and the IEA accelerated emergency releases — but a June attempt to move the same barrels drew less than 1% uptake, so the releases may not reach the market at the scale advertised. On disruption, Ukraine's strike on Rosneft's Ryazan refinery resumed a campaign against Russian diesel output even as Trump publicly condemned it, widening a rift with Kyiv at the worst possible moment for a global diesel crunch. Brent near $110 and European storage at 74% underscore that the crisis is now a products-and-diesel problem, not just a crude one — and that coal is quietly returning as the winter backstop in both Germany and South Korea.
sources: OilPrice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, IEA (Coal Mid-Year Update 2026), Rystad Energy, Energy Aspects, Times of India, Financial Times, Newsmax
